title: Blessed are you
hookLine: almost every blessing begins "blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe"

cards: Some phrases get said so often nobody hears them anymore. How are you. Bless you, after a sneeze.
Love you, at the end of a call. They're tiny, and they hold a relationship together.

Jewish life has a phrase like that, said again and again through the day: over bread, over a new fruit, after the bathroom, before lighting candles, on seeing lightning. You've heard pieces of it on this path.
Plenty of people can sing it from Hebrew school, on autopilot, without anyone ever stopping to tell them what it means. That's not a failure; it's just where today starts.

teach.b: Baruch, blessed. Atah, are you. Adonai, Lord.
Eloheinu, our God. Melech, king. Ha'olam, of the universe, or of the world.
Blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe. Then comes what it's for: who brings forth bread, who creates the fruit of the vine.
The Talmud says a blessing needs two things to count: God's name, and God's kingship. The six words carry both. Three things hide inside.
First, Adonai. It's said in place of God's four-letter name, which by long tradition isn't pronounced. Outside of prayer, Jews often avoid even Adonai and say Hashem, the Name.
Second, the grammar. It begins with you, atah, close, like talking to someone across a table.

teach.h: NEAR AS YOU, VAST AS A KING.
teach.b: Then it moves to king of the universe, vast and far. And the next words often shift to who, as if stepping back. Commentators said that's on purpose: God is both near enough to speak to and too great to hold.
Third, the puzzle. How can a person bless God, the source of blessing?

Some teachers answer that baruch here means acknowledging God as that source. Some connect the word bracha with berech, the knee, the way you bow, and with breichah, a pool of water, blessing as something that flows.

teach.h: BLESS THE LORD, O MY SOUL.
teach.b: The Psalms say, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Bless the LORD, O my soul." Six words, and before bread or lightning or anything else, the one saying them has turned toward what they call the source.

how: Blessings over food, commandments and moments open with the six-word formula baruch atah Adonai eloheinu melech ha'olam, followed by words naming the food, act or moment being blessed.

o: acknowledging God as the source of blessing
asking God to send good things to the speaker
a wish for good luck said before a long journey

games.q: what's inside the six words — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud says a blessing needs God's name and kingship
so the six words include both: Adonai eloheinu, and melech ha'olam.
Adonai is how God's four-letter name is pronounced
it's said in place of the four-letter name, which by tradition isn't pronounced.
the blessing speaks to God only as a distant king
it begins with 'you', close and personal, and then says 'king of the universe'.

games.q: you're about to bless something. the six words begin with 'you' and move to 'king of the universe'. why would the grammar shift like that?
o: God is both near and vast.
games.why: commentators say it's on purpose: close enough to speak to as 'you', too great to hold, king of the whole world.

practice: If you pray, say the six words one at a time, a breath between each: baruch, atah, Adonai, eloheinu, melech, ha'olam; if you'd rather not, hear them in your head, or say their English.
Then sit in the quiet after the sixth word, where the blessing would name what it's for.

wordCard.voice: Baruch. Blessed: the first of six words that open the everyday Jewish blessings, turning toward the source before anything else.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessed. from the same letters as bracha, a blessing, and berech, a knee.

carryVoice: Your line: six words before anything. Close as you, vast as a king. A full week, done.

sources.q: Bless the LORD, O my soul

sources.ref: Medieval commentary on the shift from you to who in blessings (e.g. the Rashba)
